semantic_correction.stem: A client with diabetes and loss of protective sensation in both feet says, "I check my feet only when they hurt." Which teaching is most appropriate?

options.A: Inspect both feet every day, including areas that are hard to see, and use a mirror or ask for help when needed.
options.B: Inspect the feet after long walks because routine daily activity is unlikely to cause unnoticed injury.
options.C: Use pain as the main warning sign because neuropathy usually makes early foot injury more noticeable.
options.D: Inspect the feet monthly unless an open sore or drainage has already appeared.

semantic_correction.rationale: The 2026 American Diabetes Association Standards of Care recommend preventive foot self-care education for people with diabetes, including those with loss of protective sensation, with daily surveillance for early foot problems using palpation or visual inspection and an unbreakable mirror when needed. Loss of protective sensation predisposes to unrecognized minor trauma, so relying on pain or infrequent inspection can delay detection of skin injury. Therefore daily inspection is the appropriate teaching.
semantic_correction.educational_objective: Teach clients with diabetic loss of protective sensation to inspect their feet every day so painless injuries or early skin changes can be identified promptly.

semantic_correction.correction_summary_append: RULE1 cleanup: removed the 'only' distractor pattern, shortened the correct answer, and retained the current ADA daily-foot-surveillance recommendation with loss-of-protective-sensation rationale.

audit_findings_append.finding: The original answer was uniquely longest and one distractor used absolute wording. The revised item directly tests daily preventive foot surveillance with balanced alternatives.

option_audit.A: Correct. It matches ADA guidance for daily foot surveillance and use of a mirror or assistance when needed.
option_audit.B: Incorrect. Loss of protective sensation can allow minor trauma from ordinary activity to go unnoticed; inspection is not limited to high-activity days.
option_audit.C: Incorrect. Neuropathy can reduce protective pain sensation, making pain an unreliable early warning sign.
option_audit.D: Incorrect. Monthly inspection is too infrequent for the daily surveillance recommended in current ADA guidance.

ambiguity_check: No second defensible answer. A alone matches the current daily-surveillance recommendation for a client with loss of protective sensation.
cueing_check: All four choices are preventive foot-care teaching statements of comparable length and specificity; no absolute-word or unique-length cue identifies A.
